Attach another OpenSAK database read-only to the SQL functions, under a schema name, so one opensak.sql() or sql_write() statement can read it together with the active database and opensak.macro_db(): `SELECT … FROM caches c JOIN found.caches f ON f.gc_code = c.gc_code`. Like GSAK's SQL `ATTACH`, which stays refused. Nothing can write to an attached database: the file is opened read- only, and SQL that would change it is refused. Without `schema`, the name is made from the database name: lower case, `_` for anything but letters and digits ("Found 2020" → `found_2020`). The schema name must be letters, digits and `_`; `main`, `temp`, `macro`, `companion` and names starting with `opensak_` are reserved. The active database cannot be attached, and neither can a database twice. Attaching the same database under the same name again does nothing. SQLite allows 10 attached databases at once, opensak.macro_db() included. The database is not updated to the current schema, so one last opened by an older OpenSAK version may lack columns; `opensak.columns("<schema>.caches")` shows what is there. Each attach prints a line in the macro output. Cannot be called inside opensak.transaction(). Stays attached after opensak.switch_database(), unless the database becomes the active one. Everything is detached when the macro ends. A macro started with opensak.run_macro() sees its caller's attached databases; what it attaches or detaches is undone when it returns. See Several databases in one query. Returns string — The schema name.

Overload.retVal: {schema: string, name: string, path: string, opensak: boolean}[]
Overload.descr: The databases attached with opensak.attach(), in the order they were attached. `opensak` is always true: only OpenSAK databases can be attached so far. Returns {schema: string, name: string, path: string, opensak: boolean}[] — One table per attached database.

The attributes of a cache, each with its `id` for opensak.update_attribute() and the fields listed under Logs, waypoints, attributes and trackables. Missing data is nil. Returns opensak.Attribute[]? — nil if the cache is not in the database.
One cache as a table (see Cache fields). It is a snapshot: changing it changes nothing in the database. Returns opensak.Cache? — The cache, or nil if it is not in the database.

Convert a cache type between GSAK's one-letter code and its name, like GSAK's CacheType(): *value* is a letter ("T"), a full name ("Traditional Cache") or a short one ("Traditional"), in any case. Returns string?, string? — The cache type and its GSAK letter (nil if it has none); nil if the type is unknown.

All cache types OpenSAK knows, with GSAK's one-letter code where GSAK has one, e.g. for a form's choice list or `filter{ type = … }`. Returns {name: string, code: string?}[] — One table per cache type.

Iterate over caches, one table per cache (see Cache fields), in a generic `for`. Without arguments: the caches of the active filter, in grid order. With filter keys (see Filter keys): the caches matching them, sorted by name; the view and the active filter stay unchanged. `all = true`: every cache of the database, sorted by name, whatever the active filter shows. `database` reads another database, without switching: its caches matching the filter keys, or all of them, sorted by name. `fields` limits the fields loaded (`code` is always included), which makes loops over many caches faster. Caches are loaded in chunks, so large databases do not hit the memory limit. Returns fun(): opensak.Cache? — Iterator for a generic `for`.

Overload.retVal: {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, saved: boolean}
Overload.descr: The active centre point, which distances and bearings are measured from. `name` is the saved centre point's name, the label of a centre set from coordinates or a cache, or "" when none was chosen; `saved` tells whether it is one of opensak.centers(). Returns {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, saved: boolean} — The active centre point.

Overload.retVal: {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, active: boolean}[]
Overload.descr: The saved centre points (Settings → User locations, with ★ Home from your geocaching.com home location first), as in the centre drop-down. `filter{ near = { point = name, km = … } }` filters by one. Returns {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, active: boolean}[] — One table per saved centre point.

A bar chart of *rows* as an SVG string, for an HTML page (opensak.html.page, opensak.write_text) or a .svg file. Each row is a table; `x` names its category field (default "key") and `y` its value field (default "count"), nil counts as 0. `horizontal = true` draws the bars from the left, for long category names. Text and grid lines take the colour of the surrounding page; the bars use the CSS variable --chart-color, else `color`. Each bar shows its value as tooltip; `labels` also writes it on the bar (default: up to 16 bars). With a list of fields as `y`, the bars are stacked, one segment per field, with a legend (`names` instead of the field names; at most 8); a matrix from opensak.stats.pivot gives one stacked bar per matrix row, e.g. finds per year and cache type. At most 5000 rows. Returns string — The chart as SVG.

Param.name: [options: {x?: string, y?: string|string[], title?: string, width?: number, height?: number, color?: string, horizontal?: boolean, labels?: boolean, names?: string[]}]

Overload.descr: A grid chart of a matrix (see opensak.stats.pivot) as an SVG string: one cell per row × column value, the darker the larger, e.g. finds per difficulty × terrain. `labels = false` leaves the numbers out of the cells; `row_title` and `col_title` name the two fields. Returns string — The chart as SVG.

Param.name: [options: {title?: string, width?: number, color?: string, labels?: boolean, row_title?: string, col_title?: string}]

Overload.descr: A line chart of *rows* in their order as an SVG string, like opensak.chart.bar: `x` the label on the x axis (evenly spaced, e.g. months), `y` the value. `area = true` fills below the line. The value of the last point is written next to it unless `labels = false`. Each point shows its value as tooltip. Returns string — The chart as SVG.

Param.name: [options: {x?: string, y?: string, title?: string, width?: number, height?: number, color?: string, area?: boolean, labels?: boolean}]

Overload.descr: A map of countries, states or counties as an SVG string, each region coloured by a value — e.g. finds per country from opensak.stats.group. `key` names the field with the region name (default "key"), `value` the number (default "count"), `layer` the kind of region: "country" (default), "state" or "county". `within` (a country name or a list) limits a state or county map to those countries; without it the countries the regions are in are shown. `extent = "all"` shows every region of the layer instead of zooming to the ones with a value. Names are matched ignoring case, accents and punctuation; those that match no region are listed below the map. The outlines are those of Update location (offline, no internet needed; county outlines are downloaded per country on first use, like there). Without the boundary data the map is a short note instead. Returns string — The map as SVG.

Param.name: [options: {key?: string, value?: string, layer?: string, within?: string|string[], title?: string, width?: number, height?: number, color?: string, extent?: string, legend?: boolean}]

Overload.descr: A dot map as an SVG string: one dot per row at its coordinates (fields `lat` and `lon`), over the outlines of `layer` ("country", "state" or "county"), zoomed to the dots or to the `within` countries. `label` names the field shown as tooltip. At most 50000 rows; dots on the same pixel are drawn once. Returns string — The map as SVG.

Param.name: [options: {lat?: string, lon?: string, label?: string, layer?: string, within?: string|string[], title?: string, width?: number, height?: number, color?: string, radius?: number}]

Overload.descr: A rose (polar area) chart of *rows* as an SVG string: one sector per row, in row order clockwise from the top, e.g. finds per compass direction (N, NE, E, …). The area of a sector grows with its value; `x` names the label field, `y` the value (as for opensak.chart.bar). Returns string — The chart as SVG.

Param.name: [options: {x?: string, y?: string, title?: string, width?: number, color?: string, labels?: boolean}]

Overload.descr: Let the user pick one item of a list. Returns string|number? — The item picked, or nil if cancelled.

Let the user pick a file in a file dialog. The picked file may be used for the rest of this run without a folder permission: read with mode "open" (the default), written with mode "save". OpenSAK's own settings and database files cannot be picked. The dialog starts in the macro file's folder. Returns string? — Full path of the picked file, or nil if cancelled.

Let the user pick a folder in a folder dialog. The macro may then read and write files in it for the rest of this run, without a folder permission. OpenSAK's own folders and whole drives cannot be picked. Returns string? — Full path of the folder, or nil if cancelled.
Remove the corrected coordinates of a cache. Returns boolean — false if the cache is not in the database.
Remove the active filter, so all caches are shown again.
The GC codes of the caches of the active filter, in grid order. Cheaper than opensak.caches() when only the codes are needed. Returns string[] — GC codes.

The columns of a table or view of the active database (or the one named by the `database` option). Returns {name: string, type: string, required: boolean}[] — Column names and SQL types, in table order; `required`: NOT NULL without a default, so an INSERT must give it.
Ask the user a Yes/No question. Returns boolean — true on Yes.

Initial bearing from the first point to the second. Returns number — Degrees, 0 = North, clockwise.

Great-circle distance between two points. Returns number — Distance in km.

Format coordinates. Formats: `"dmm"` (default), `"dms"`, `"dd"`, `"utm"`, `"mgrs"`, `"ch1903"` (Swiss LV03), `"ch1903+"` (Swiss LV95), `"rd"` (Dutch RD), `"osgb"` (British National Grid), `"sweref99"` (SWEREF 99 TM), `"gk"` (German Gauss-Krüger), `"olc"` (Plus Code), `"geohash"` and `"maidenhead"`. Aliases: `"lv03"`, `"lv95"`, `"bng"`, `"sweref"`, `"gauss-krueger"`, `"pluscode"`, `"qth"`. The national grids are only meaningful in and around their country; `"osgb"` and `"utm"` raise an error where they are not defined. Returns string — E.g. "N47 22.123 E008 32.456" or "32T E 465123 N 5247123".

Format coordinates. Formats: `"dmm"` (default), `"dms"`, `"dd"`, `"utm"`, `"mgrs"`, `"ch1903"` (Swiss LV03), `"ch1903+"` (Swiss LV95), `"rd"` (Dutch RD), `"osgb"` (British National Grid), `"sweref99"` (SWEREF 99 TM), `"gk"` (German Gauss-Krüger), `"olc"` (Plus Code), `"geohash"` and `"maidenhead"`. Aliases: `"lv03"`, `"lv95"`, `"bng"`, `"sweref"`, `"gauss-krueger"`, `"pluscode"`, `"qth"`. The national grids are only meaningful in and around their country; `"osgb"` and `"utm"` raise an error where they are not defined. Returns string — E.g. "N47 22.123 E008 32.456" or "32T E 465123 N 5247123".

Whether a point lies inside a polygon. The polygon is either a file (GPX track/route/waypoints, KML, or a text file with one coordinate per line; read permission needed, relative paths are resolved against the macro file's folder) or a table of points, each a coordinate string, `{lat, lon}` or `{lat = ..., lon = ...}`. Edges are straight lines in latitude/longitude, as in the line/polygon filter. Returns boolean — true if the point is inside.

Whether a point lies inside a polygon. The polygon is either a file (GPX track/route/waypoints, KML, or a text file with one coordinate per line; read permission needed, relative paths are resolved against the macro file's folder) or a table of points, each a coordinate string, `{lat, lon}` or `{lat = ..., lon = ...}`. Edges are straight lines in latitude/longitude, as in the line/polygon filter. Returns boolean — true if the point is inside.

Offline reverse geocoding with the boundary data used by Update location. A field is nil where no region matches. Returns {country: string?, state: string?, county: string?}? — nil if the boundary data is not installed.

Offline reverse geocoding with the boundary data used by Update location. A field is nil where no region matches. Returns {country: string?, state: string?, county: string?}? — nil if the boundary data is not installed.
The point halfway between two points (along the great circle). Returns number, number — Latitude and longitude of the midpoint.
The point halfway between two points (along the great circle). Returns number, number — Latitude and longitude of the midpoint.

Parse a coordinate string. Without `fmt` the format is detected: latitude/longitude (DMM, DMS, decimal degrees), UTM, MGRS, British grid letters ("TQ 30268 79642"), Plus Codes, Maidenhead locators, geohashes (5+ characters mixing letters and digits) and the Swiss, Dutch, Swedish and German grids as number pairs, which are only accepted inside their country. Pass `fmt` to read one format only — needed for numeric British grid positions, short geohashes and to rule out a wrong guess. Formats: `"latlon"`, `"utm"`, `"mgrs"`, `"ch1903"`, `"rd"`, `"osgb"`, `"sweref99"`, `"gk"`, `"olc"`, `"geohash"`, `"maidenhead"` (`"latlon"` covers DD, DMM and DMS; every name `opensak.coords.format` takes works too). Returns number?, number?, string? — Latitude, longitude and the format that was read, or nil if the text cannot be parsed.
Waypoint projection: the point a given distance away in a given direction. Returns number, number — Latitude and longitude of the projected point.
Waypoint projection: the point a given distance away in a given direction. Returns number, number — Latitude and longitude of the projected point.
Like opensak.move_caches(), but the caches stay in the active database. Returns integer — Number of caches copied.

Copy a file (GSAK's FileCopy) and return the file written. *target* is a file, or a folder (existing, or ending in `/`) to copy into under the same name. Relative paths are resolved against the macro file's folder. The source's folder needs read permission and the target's folder write permission; for an unapproved one the user is asked first. Only these file types can be written: .txt .csv .tsv .html .htm .svg .md .json .gpx .loc .kml .kmz .ggz .zip .xml .log .jpg .jpeg .png .gif .webp .pdf — no programs or scripts. An existing target is replaced, the same way opensak.write_text() replaces a file, unless `if_exists = "skip"`. The modification time is kept. At most 1 GB. Returns string? — The file written (full path); nil if skipped.
The number of caches matching the active filter. Returns integer — Number of caches shown.

Create a new, empty database in the default database folder and add it to the list. The active database does not change. Fails if the name is taken or its file already exists. Returns string — The name actually used (surrounding spaces removed).

Create a folder, with any missing folders above it, and return it. A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. The folder it goes into needs write permission; for an unapproved one the user is asked first. A folder that exists already is fine. Returns string — The folder (full path).
The cache selected in the grid. Returns opensak.Cache? — The cache, or nil if no row is selected.
The name of the active database. Returns string — Database name.
Whether a database with this name is in the database list (exact, case-sensitive match). Returns boolean — true if it exists.

Overload.retVal: {name: string, path: string, active: boolean, size_mb: number}[]
Overload.descr: All databases in OpenSAK's database list, sorted by name. Returns {name: string, path: string, active: boolean, size_mb: number}[] — One table per database.
Whole days from date *a* to date *b* (negative if *b* is earlier). Dates are "YYYY-MM-DD" strings (a time after it is ignored) or seconds since the epoch. Returns integer — Days.
Format seconds since the epoch (e.g. from `os.time()` or `opensak.date.parse()`) in local time. Returns string — The formatted date.

Parse a date into seconds since the epoch, the same kind of value as `os.time()`. Without a format, ISO 8601 (`"2026-10-06"`, `"2026-10-06T14:30:00Z"`) and `"06.10.2026 [14:30[:00]]"` are understood. Times without a zone are local time. Returns integer? — Seconds since the epoch, or nil if the text does not parse.

The period a date falls in, named as opensak.stats.group names it: "day" ("2026-10-06"), "week" ("2026-W41"), "month" ("2026-10"), "year" ("2026") or "weekday" ("Tue"). For a field of your own to group or pivot by, e.g. the year × month table of your finds. Returns string — The period.

Delete caches from the active database, each with its logs, waypoints, attributes, trackables and user note, like Waypoint → Delete cache. Takes one GC code, or a list of them, e.g. opensak.codes() for the caches of the active filter. Deleted caches cannot be restored from inside OpenSAK (only from a backup); at the end of the run the macro output says how many caches were deleted. The cache list and map drop them after the macro. Locked caches are deleted too: the lock only protects from imports. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean|integer — For one code: false if the cache is not in the database. For a list: the number of caches deleted.

Delete caches from the active database, each with its logs, waypoints, attributes, trackables and user note, like Waypoint → Delete cache. Takes one GC code, or a list of them, e.g. opensak.codes() for the caches of the active filter. Deleted caches cannot be restored from inside OpenSAK (only from a backup); at the end of the run the macro output says how many caches were deleted. The cache list and map drop them after the macro. Locked caches are deleted too: the lock only protects from imports. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean|integer — For one code: false if the cache is not in the database. For a list: the number of caches deleted.
Delete a attribute from the active database. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean — false if there is no attribute with this id.

Delete a file (GSAK's FileErase). A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. Its folder needs write permission; for an unapproved one the user is asked first. Only the file types opensak.copy_file() writes can be deleted, never a folder, a link or OpenSAK's own files. Returns boolean — false if the file did not exist.

Delete an empty folder; a folder with anything in it is an error, so delete its files first. The folder it is in needs write permission. A folder listed in Settings → Folder permissions is never deleted. Returns boolean — false if the folder did not exist.
Delete a log from the active database. OpenSAK updates the cache's log counts and dates. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean — false if there is no log with this id.

Delete a trackable from the active database. OpenSAK updates the cache's trackable count. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean — false if there is no trackable with this id.

Delete a waypoint from the active database. OpenSAK updates the cache's waypoint count. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean — false if there is no waypoint with this id.

The listing description of a cache. Not part of the cache table because it can be large. Returns {short: string?, long: string?, html: boolean}? — Short and long description and whether they are HTML; nil if the cache is not in the database.
Detach a database attached with opensak.attach(). Optional: everything is detached when the macro ends. Cannot be called inside opensak.transaction().
End the macro right away. pcall cannot catch it, and it is not an error: the macro window shows the code, and `opensak --run-macro` exits with it.

Export the caches of the active filter with a saved export setting (File → Export → GPX/LOC/GGZ: format, folder, file name, if the file exists, corrected coordinates, max. caches). The file name variables are filled in as in the dialog, {filter} with the name of the active filter and {center} with the active centre point. The file goes into *folder* if given, else into the setting's folder. That folder needs write permission (Settings → Folder permissions); for an unapproved one the user is asked first. Nothing is written when no cache with coordinates is shown, or when the file exists and the setting says skip (or ask, and the user answers No). Returns string?, integer? — The file written and the number of caches in it; nil if nothing was written.

Export the caches of the active filter without a saved export setting. `path` is the file to write; its name may use the variables of the export dialog ({database}, {filter}, {center}, {date}, {count}, ...), and a relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. Its folder needs write permission, like opensak.export_file(). `rename(c)` and `description(c)` are called with each cache table (see Cache fields) and return the name and the waypoint description to write (nil keeps the default). With `target = "device"`, the file goes into the GPX or GGZ folder of the connected Garmin device instead (`path` is then only the file name; MTP devices are not supported yet). Nothing is written when no cache with coordinates is shown, or when the file exists and `if_exists` says skip (or ask, and the user answers No). Returns string?, integer? — The file written and the number of caches in it; nil if nothing was written.

Export the caches of the active filter and/or their child waypoints as Garmin POI files (.gpi) with a saved POI export setting (File → Export Garmin POI: folder, file name, if the file exists, which points, name/description/extra templates, category, proximity alert, icon, max. points). The file name variables are filled in as in the dialog. With "one file per waypoint type" a file is written for the caches and one for every waypoint type. The files go into *folder* if given, else into the setting's folder, which needs write permission (Settings → Folder permissions); for an unapproved one the user is asked first. An existing file is skipped when the setting says skip (or ask, and the user answers No). Returns string[]?, integer? — The files written and the number of POIs in them; nil if nothing was written.

Whether a file exists (false for a folder). A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. The folder needs read permission, like opensak.read_text(). Returns boolean — true if the file exists.

Overload.retVal: {name: string, path: string, dir: boolean, size: integer, modified: integer}?
Overload.descr: Size and modification time of one file or folder, as in opensak.list_dir(); nil if it does not exist. A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. The folder needs read permission. Returns {name: string, path: string, dir: boolean, size: integer, modified: integer}? — nil if there is nothing at *path*.

Build a filter from the given keys (see Filter keys; combined with AND unless `mode = "OR"`) and apply it. Usually called with table syntax: `opensak.filter{ ... }`. When nothing matches, the view is left unchanged. Returns integer — Number of matching caches (0 = view unchanged).

The name of the active filter: the `label` of opensak.filter{}, a profile name, or "" when no filter is active. The same as the {filter} variable of an export file name. Returns string — The filter name; "" for none.
Apply a saved filter profile. Returns integer — Number of matching caches.
Whether a folder exists. A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. The folder containing it needs read permission. Returns boolean — true if the folder exists.

Show a dialog built from a table (see Forms) and wait until it is closed. Fields with a value come back in a table keyed by their `id`. Callbacks such as `on_change` run while the form stays open and can change it through the handle they get. Without `buttons` the form has OK and Cancel. Tools → Form designer in the macro window builds forms visually and imports GSAK forms. Returns table<string, any>?, string? — The values by field id and the id of the button (or `exit_on_change` field, or "timeout") that closed the form; nil if it was cancelled.

The outlines of countries, states or counties (`layer`) as a GeoJSON FeatureCollection (a table), e.g. for a map drawn by the macro itself or for another program. Like opensak.chart.map, `rows` puts the value (field `value`, default "count") of each row into the properties of the region its field `key` (default "key") names — matched ignoring case, accents and punctuation — `within` limits the countries and `extent = "all"` shows all regions instead of zooming to the ones with a value. `around` (rows with `lat`/`lon`) zooms to those points instead, `box` (`{min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat}`, e.g. the `bbox` of another collection) to an area. The outlines are clipped to the area and simplified for a map about `detail` pixels wide (default 800). Every feature has `properties.name` (and `country` for states and counties). The second value lists the names that match no region. nil if the boundary data is not installed. Returns table?, string[]? — The FeatureCollection and the names without a region.

Param.name: [options: {within?: string|string[], rows?: table[], key?: string, value?: string, extent?: string, around?: table[], lat?: string, lon?: string, box?: number[], detail?: number}]

Overload.descr: The regions of a layer ("country", "state" or "county") in the boundary data used by Update location and opensak.chart.map, one row per name: `{name =}`, for states and counties also `country`. `within` limits them to one country or a list. With `rows` (e.g. finds per state from opensak.stats.group) the rows are matched to the regions like opensak.chart.map does — the field `key` (default "key") names the region, ignoring case, accents and punctuation — and a region named by rows gets the sum of their field `value` (default "count"); the second value then lists the names that match no region. With it a macro can say "18 of 26 cantons". nil if the boundary data is not installed. Returns {name: string, country?: string}[]?, string[]? — The regions, sorted (with `rows`: and the names that match none).

Param.name: [options: {within?: string|string[], rows?: table[], key?: string, value?: string}]

Overload.descr: Put HTML parts (e.g. two tables) side by side; on a narrow window they go one below the other. Returns string — HTML.
*value* as text for HTML: `& < > " '` are escaped, nil becomes "", 3.0 becomes "3". Returns string — Escaped text.

A matrix (from opensak.stats.pivot) as an HTML table: the values of the two fields as headings, each cell shaded by its value. `percent = true` shows each cell as a share of all, `totals = true` adds a total row and column, `shade = false` leaves the colours out; `row_title` and `col_title` name the fields, `color` ("#rrggbb") the shading. Inline styles only, so the shading also shows without the stylesheet of opensak.html.page. Returns string — HTML.

Param.name: [options: {shade?: boolean, percent?: boolean, totals?: boolean, row_title?: string, col_title?: string, color?: string}]

Overload.descr: A complete HTML page for opensak.write_text: `title` (also the heading), `subtitle`, the body — the strings in the list part of the table, and/or `body` — and `footer`. A built-in stylesheet with a light and a dark theme styles headings (`<h2>`), tables, tiles and columns; `css` is added after it. The body is put in as it is: build it from the html.* functions, or escape your own text with html.escape. Returns string — The page.

Param.name: spec: {title?: string, subtitle?: string, css?: string, lang?: string, footer?: string, body?: string|string[], [integer]: string}

Overload.descr: *rows* as an HTML table (values escaped), e.g. the rows of opensak.sql() (GSAK's SqlToHtml). `columns` lists the fields to show, each a field name or `{field, heading}`; without it all fields are shown, sorted by name — a Lua table has no field order, so pass `columns` to keep the order of the query. Number columns are right-aligned. `link = { code = "url" }` turns the code cells into links to the row's url field (http/https only). `bars = {"count"}` adds a bar next to each value of those number fields, scaled to the largest (in `color`, "#rrggbb"). The bars use inline styles only, so they also show without the stylesheet of opensak.html.page. Returns string — HTML.

Param.name: [options: {columns?: (string|string[])[], link?: table<string, string>, caption?: string, bars?: string[], color?: string}]

Overload.descr: Key figures as a row of tiles: a list of `{label =, value =}`. Returns string — HTML.

Import GPX files and Pocket Query zips without any question (like File → Import GPX / PQ zip, then Import) and return what was done. *source* is the name of an import setting saved in that dialog — its files, folders and target database are used — or else the path of a `.gpx` / `.zip` file or of a folder. A folder imports every GPX / zip file directly in it (not in subfolders), looked up at each run, so the folder Pocket Queries are downloaded to can be imported every night. A GPX file's waypoints file next to it is imported with it. A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder, and environment variables such as `%USERPROFILE%` are expanded; the files need read permission. The caches go into `database` if given, else the setting's database, else the active one. Files and folders of a setting that no longer exist are left out and listed in `missing`; a file that fails is reported and the others are still imported. Cancel stops after the current file. Unlike the dialog, country and state are not looked up afterwards (reverse geocoding). The summary is printed (unless `quiet`) and written to the log file. Returns opensak.GpxImportReport — What was imported, per file.

Import GSAK databases without any question (like File → Import GSAK database, with the answers given up front) and return what was done. *source* is a GSAK backup .zip, a GSAK folder (the install / data folder with `gsak.db3` and `data/<name>/sqlite.db3`, its `data` folder, or one database's folder), a single `.db3` cache database (just that database), or `gsak.db3` (only user locations and saved filters). A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder, and environment variables such as `%APPDATA%` are expanded; the folder needs read permission. Each GSAK database goes into the OpenSAK database of the same name, created if missing, unless `target` says otherwise. For an OpenSAK database that exists, `if_exists` decides: `"skip"` (default), `"merge"` (new caches added, existing ones updated, locked caches kept) or `"overwrite"` (emptied first). `filters` and `locations` also import the saved filters and user locations of `gsak.db3`; `true` skips the ones whose name exists when `if_exists` is `"skip"` and replaces them otherwise. Embedded note images are replaced by placeholders without asking. A database that fails is reported and the others are still imported. The summary is printed (unless `quiet`) and written to the log file. Returns opensak.GsakImportReport — What was imported, per database.
Whether the macro is inside opensak.transaction(). Returns boolean — true inside opensak.transaction().
Ask for one line of text. Returns string? — The text entered, or nil if cancelled.

Add a new cache to the active database. `code`, `name`, `type`, `lat` and `lon` are required; any other writable field may be given too (see Changing caches). Fails if the code is already in the database. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns string — The cache code as stored (upper case).

Add a attribute to a cache in the active database; `attribute_id` required. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns integer? — The new attribute's id; nil if the cache is not in the database.

Add a log to a cache in the active database; `type` required. OpenSAK updates the cache's log counts and dates. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns integer? — The new log's id; nil if the cache is not in the database.

Add a trackable to a cache in the active database. OpenSAK updates the cache's trackable count. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns integer? — The new trackable's id; nil if the cache is not in the database.

Add a waypoint to a cache in the active database; `prefix`, `type` required. OpenSAK updates the cache's waypoint count. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns integer? — The new waypoint's id; nil if the cache is not in the database.

Overload.retVal: {name: string, path: string, dir: boolean, size: integer, modified: integer}[]
Overload.descr: The files and folders in a folder (not in its subfolders), sorted by name. A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. The folder needs read permission; for an unapproved one the user is asked first. `pattern` keeps the names that match it, ignoring case: `*` stands for any text, `?` for one character. At most 10,000 entries. Each entry has `name`, `path` (full path), `dir` (true for a folder), `size` (bytes, 0 for a folder) and `modified` (seconds since the epoch, like `os.time()`). Returns {name: string, path: string, dir: boolean, size: integer, modified: integer}[] — One table per entry.
Write a message to OpenSAK's log file and the macro output. Run with `opensak --run-macro`, it goes to stderr while print() goes to stdout.

The logs of a cache, each with its `id` for opensak.update_log() and the fields listed under Logs, waypoints, attributes and trackables. Missing data is nil. Returns opensak.Log[]? — nil if the cache is not in the database.

Attach the macro's own SQLite database — a file named after the macro file with the extension .db3, in the macro's folder, created if missing — to the SQL functions as schema `macro`. In it the macro has full access through opensak.sql(), sql_each() and sql_write(): CREATE, DROP, ALTER, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on `macro.<name>` tables, indexes, views and triggers, and `PRAGMA macro.user_version`. Its data stays between runs. One statement can read and write the active database and the macro database together, e.g. `INSERT INTO macro.seen SELECT gc_code FROM caches`; the rules for the active database stay the same. Unqualified names mean the active database first, so create with `macro.` in front. opensak.tables() lists its tables as `macro.<name>`. The macro's folder must be writable for macros, like any file a macro writes (Settings → Folder permissions; the macros folder is by default); otherwise OpenSAK asks the user to allow it, and a denial makes the call fail. The first call creates the file, even if nothing is written to it, and prints its path in the macro output. OpenSAK remembers the file, and its backups include it in `macro_databases/`, wherever it is. If the folder cannot be written the call fails; a read-only file can be read but not changed. Unlike opensak.update() it needs no approval to change databases (see Changing caches). Changes inside opensak.transaction() are kept or undone together with those of the active database. The SQL statement ATTACH itself stays refused. Cannot be called inside opensak.transaction(); stays attached after opensak.switch_database(). The macro must be saved, as the file is named after it. In a macro started with opensak.run_macro() it attaches the called macro's own file instead; the caller's file is attached again when the called macro returns. Returns string — The path of the macro database file.

Set, clear or swap the macro flag (field `macro_flag`) of many caches at once, like GSAK's MACROFLAG: the caches of the active filter, the given GC code(s), or `{ all = true }` for every cache of the active database. The macro flag is the macros' own, separate from the user flag; filter with `filter{ macro_flag = true }`. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns integer — The number of caches whose flag changed.
OpenSAK's macros folder (read permission by default), without a trailing separator. Returns string — Folder path.
Show a message with an OK button and wait until the user closes it.

Move caches from the active database to another one, with all logs, waypoints, attributes, trackables and notes (like Database → Move caches). By default the caches of the active filter. When a cache already exists in the target, `if_exists` decides: `"newer"` (default) replaces it only if the active database's copy was imported later, `"replace"` always, `"skip"` never. A cache not written to the target stays in the active database. Returns integer — Number of caches moved.

Move or rename a file: like opensak.copy_file(), then the source is deleted, so its folder needs write permission too and it must be one of the file types listed there. Nothing is copied when the source may not be deleted. Returns string? — The new file (full path); nil if skipped (the source is then kept).

Open a file in its default app, e.g. an HTML report in the browser, so a report macro can end by showing its result. A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. A file this run wrote (opensak.write_text, opensak.export_*, opensak.copy_file / move_file) or one in opensak.temp_dir() opens directly; for any other file the user is asked first. Only these file types: .html .htm .svg .txt .csv .tsv .md .json .gpx .kml .pdf — never a program, script or shortcut — and no URLs. At most 5 files per run. Needs the user interface.
The names of all saved filter profiles. Returns string[] — Profile names.

Open a progress window with a Cancel button, for long loops. `p:update(i [, text])` moves the bar to *i* of *total* and returns false once the user has pressed Cancel; `p:close()` closes the window (also done when the macro ends). Without *total* the bar just shows that work is going on. Returns opensak.Progress — The window.
Escape every character that has a meaning in a regular expression, so the text matches literally (GSAK's RegExEscape), e.g. to search for a cache name in a pattern. Returns string — The escaped text.

Search for the first match of a regular expression (Python syntax). Each call may run at most 2 s. Returns string?, string?... — The whole match followed by the captures (nil for a group that did not take part), or nil if there is no match.

All non-overlapping matches. Without capture groups each item is the whole match, with one group it is the capture, with several it is an array of the captures. Returns string[]|string[][] — The matches.
Whether the text contains a match. Use `^` and `$` to match the whole text. Returns boolean — true if the pattern matches.

Replace matches. In a replacement string, `\1` or `\g<name>` insert a capture. A replacement function gets the whole match and the captures and returns the new text (nil or false keeps the match). Returns string, integer — The new text and the number of replacements.
Split the text at every non-empty match. Returns string[] — The pieces between the matches.

Read a CSV file (UTF-8) into an array of rows keyed by the header line. A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. If the file's folder has no read permission (Settings → Folder permissions), OpenSAK asks the user to allow it for this run or always. The file may be at most 10 MB. Returns table<string, string>[] — One table per data row, keyed by header.

Read a whole text file, of any file type. A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. The folder needs read permission; for an unapproved one the user is asked first. UTF-8 unless `encoding` says otherwise (`"utf-8"`, `"latin-1"`, `"cp1252"`); a UTF-8 byte order mark is removed and line endings become `"\n"`. At most 10 MB. Returns string — The file's text.
Redraw the cache list, detail panel and map now. Changes a macro makes are otherwise shown when it ends.

Apply a filter saved with opensak.save_filter(), like GSAK's RestoreFilter(). As with opensak.filter{}, the view is left unchanged when nothing matches. A filter saved while none was active clears the filter. Returns integer — Number of matching caches (0 = view unchanged, unless the saved filter was empty).

Recalculate now the columns OpenSAK maintains itself (distance and bearing, log, waypoint and trackable counts, log dates) for the caches changed so far in the open opensak.transaction(). Inside a transaction they are recalculated only once, just before the commit, which makes many writes much faster; until then opensak.cache, sql and the like still see the old values. Call resync() when a later read inside the transaction depends on them. Outside a transaction it does nothing, as every write is recalculated before its own commit. Returns integer — Number of caches recalculated (0 outside a transaction).

Run another macro and wait until it has finished, e.g. to chain several macros from one control macro. A relative path is looked up in the folder of the calling macro, and `.lua` is added when the name has no extension. The called macro gets its own global variables; values are passed as extra arguments (read them with `...`) and come back as its return values. An error in it stops the calling macro too, unless caught with `pcall`. Macros run this way share the run's limits, sleep time and folder approvals; they may call each other at most 10 levels deep. Returns any... — What the macro returns.

The active filter (with its name, and any quick filter or search box) as a string, to put back later with opensak.restore_filter() — e.g. to leave the user's filter as it was after the macro filtered for its own work. Like GSAK's SaveFilter(). The sort order is not included. The string can be stored with opensak.settings.save(); don't build or change it. Returns string — The saved filter; when no filter is active, restoring it clears the filter.
Select a cache in the cache list and show it in the detail panel and on the map, like a click on its row. Returns boolean — false if the cache is not among the caches of the active filter.
The GC codes of the rows selected in the grid. Returns string[] — GC codes; empty if nothing is selected.

Overload.retVal: {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, saved: boolean}
Overload.descr: Change the active centre point, like the centre drop-down in the toolbar (GSAK's Centre): a saved centre point by name, or coordinates with an optional name to show. Coordinates are not saved as a user location. Distance and bearing of every cache in the active database are recalculated and stored, so the macro needs permission to change the database, and it cannot be used inside opensak.transaction(). The centre stays when the macro ends. Returns {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, saved: boolean} — The new centre point, as opensak.center() returns it.

Overload.retVal: {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, saved: boolean}
Overload.descr: Change the active centre point, like the centre drop-down in the toolbar (GSAK's Centre): a saved centre point by name, or coordinates with an optional name to show. Coordinates are not saved as a user location. Distance and bearing of every cache in the active database are recalculated and stored, so the macro needs permission to change the database, and it cannot be used inside opensak.transaction(). The centre stays when the macro ends. Returns {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, saved: boolean} — The new centre point, as opensak.center() returns it.

Overload.retVal: {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, saved: boolean}
Overload.descr: Change the active centre point, like the centre drop-down in the toolbar (GSAK's Centre): a saved centre point by name, or coordinates with an optional name to show. Coordinates are not saved as a user location. Distance and bearing of every cache in the active database are recalculated and stored, so the macro needs permission to change the database, and it cannot be used inside opensak.transaction(). The centre stays when the macro ends. Returns {name: string, lat: number, lon: number, saved: boolean} — The new centre point, as opensak.center() returns it.

Set corrected coordinates, either as decimal degrees or as one coordinate string in any format OpenSAK understands (DMM, DMS, decimal degrees). Returns boolean — false if the cache is not in the database.

Set corrected coordinates, either as decimal degrees or as one coordinate string in any format OpenSAK understands (DMM, DMS, decimal degrees). Returns boolean — false if the cache is not in the database.
Remove this macro's saved settings, so the next opensak.settings.load() returns an empty table.

The settings this macro saved with opensak.settings.save(), or an empty table on the first run. Each macro has its own settings, kept per macro file in the `settings` folder of the macros folder; no other macro can read them. A renamed macro starts with empty settings, and an unsaved macro has none. Returns table — The saved settings; empty if there are none.

Save settings for the next run of this macro, replacing the saved ones. Strings, numbers, booleans and nested tables can be saved; a table needs string keys, or 1, 2, 3, … for a list. Functions and cyclic tables are refused, and the settings may take up at most 1 MB.
Pause the macro. One pause lasts at most 10 s and all pauses of a run together at most 60 s; a cancelled macro stops at its next pause.

Sort the cache list, like a click on a column header. opensak.caches() and opensak.codes() then return the caches in this order. Fields: `name`, `code`, `type`, `container`, `difficulty`, `terrain`, `hidden`, `placed_by`, `country`, `state`, `county`, `found`, `found_date`, `dnf`, `dnf_date`, `ftf`, `archived`, `premium`, `distance`, `bearing`, `favorite_points`, `trackable_count`, `user_flag`, `locked`, `user_sort`, `user_data1`, `user_data2`, `user_data3`, `user_data4`, `macro_sort`. `macro_sort` has no column in the cache list, so no column header shows the sort; it compares as text, so pad numbers ("0042").

Run a read-only SQL query (SQLite) against the active database (or the one named by the `database` option) and return all rows. Only reading statements are allowed, except on TEMP tables: a macro may create, fill, change and drop its own TEMP tables, views and indexes (`CREATE TEMP TABLE ...`) and use them in any query, opensak.sql_write() included. They are never stored in the database and are gone when the macro ends or calls opensak.switch_database(); changes to them inside opensak.transaction() are undone with it. A TEMP table may not take the name of a table of the database. Column names follow the database schema, which may change between versions (see opensak.tables() and opensak.columns()). Use `AS` to name computed columns. NULL values are nil. At most 100,000 rows; use opensak.sql_each() for more. A query is aborted after 60 s. Returns table<string, any>[] — One table per row, keyed by column name.
Like opensak.sql(), but returns an iterator for a generic `for` that fetches the rows in chunks — for results of any size. Returns fun(): table<string, any>? — Iterator for a generic `for`.

Run one INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE statement (SQLite) against the active database — the power tool for bulk work, changing many rows with one statement. For a single cache or row, prefer `opensak.update()`, `insert{}`, `delete()`, `insert_<x>()`, `update_<x>()` and `delete_<x>()`, which check each field and need no knowledge of the schema (see Changing caches). Only the cache tables can be changed (`attributes`, `caches`, `logs`, `trackables`, `user_notes`, `waypoints`), and an UPDATE may not set the keys or the columns OpenSAK maintains itself (see Changing caches). Deleting a cache also deletes its logs, waypoints, attributes, trackables and user note, as opensak.delete() does. Locked caches are changed and deleted like any other (add `AND locked = 0` to leave them alone). REPLACE (`INSERT OR REPLACE`, `REPLACE INTO`, …) is refused, as it would delete those too; to update or insert, use `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (gc_code) DO UPDATE SET …`. OpenSAK recalculates distances, counts and log dates of the caches the statement touched — inside opensak.transaction() once at its end (see opensak.resync()). An INSERT only needs the real data: the columns opensak.columns() marks as `required`, e.g. `gc_code`, `name`, `cache_type`, `latitude` and `longitude` for a cache (see Changing caches); every other column gets its default. Each statement is committed on its own (or with the surrounding opensak.transaction()), or not at all on an error. BEGIN, COMMIT and the like are refused; use opensak.transaction(). Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns integer — Number of rows inserted, updated or deleted (without the rows deleted along with a cache).

Every *step*-th row of *rows*, e.g. every 1000th find (sort the rows first, see opensak.stats.sort): copies with the row number in `n`. The first and the last row are included unless `first = false` / `last = false`. With `date = field`, `days` holds the days since the previous row picked. Returns table[] — Copies of the picked rows.

*rows* sorted by the period in field `key` (default "key"), with a row added for each missing "day", "month" (default) or "year" between the first and the last row, or between `from` and `to`. Number fields of an added row are 0. Use it before a chart or table over time, so months without finds still take their place. Returns table[] — New rows.

Param.name: [options: {key?: string, period?: string, from?: string, to?: string}]

Overload.retVal: {key: any, count: integer, distinct?: integer, sum?: number}[]
Overload.descr: Count *rows* per value of the field *by* and return one row per group: `{key =, count =}`, sorted by key. Rows can come from opensak.caches(), opensak.sql() or opensak.read_csv(); rows whose *by* is nil are left out. Options: `period` groups a date field ("YYYY-MM-DD" or os.time() seconds) by "day", "week" ("2026-W41"), "month" ("2026-10"), "year" or "weekday" ("Mon"…"Sun", sorted Monday first). `count_distinct = field` adds `distinct`, the number of different values of that field per group; `sum = field` adds `sum`. `sort = "count"` (or "sum") puts the largest group first. `top = n` keeps n groups and puts the rest into one group named `other` (default "Other"). Returns {key: any, count: integer, distinct?: integer, sum?: number}[] — One row per group.

Param.name: [options: {period?: string, count_distinct?: string, sum?: string, sort?: string, top?: integer, other?: string}]

Overload.descr: Count *rows* per pair of values of two fields, e.g. difficulty × terrain. Returns `{rows =, cols =, cells =, max =, total =, filled =}`: `rows` and `cols` are the values of the two fields (sorted), `cells[i][j]` the count for rows[i] and cols[j], `filled` the number of cells that are not 0. The options `rows` and `cols` give the values and their order instead (other values are left out); `sum = field` adds up that field instead of counting. For opensak.html.matrix. Returns opensak.Matrix — The matrix.
Copies of *rows* with the running total of *field* (default "count") in *into* (default "total"), e.g. the total number of finds at the end of each month. Returns table[] — New rows.

A new list of *rows* sorted by the fields in turn; "-field" sorts largest first. nil values come last. Faster than table.sort with a compare function, and stable: rows with equal fields keep their order. Returns table[] — The same rows in the new order.

Overload.retVal: {days: integer, longest?: opensak.Run, gap?: opensak.Run, last?: opensak.Run}
Overload.descr: Runs of days in a date field: `days` (the number of different days), `longest` (most days in a row with at least one row, e.g. your longest caching streak), `gap` (most days in a row without, between the first and the last day) and `last` (the run that ends on the last day). Each run is `{days =, first =, last =}`; `gap` is nil if there is none. Returns {days: integer, longest?: opensak.Run, gap?: opensak.Run, last?: opensak.Run} — The runs.

Overload.retVal: {count: integer, distinct: integer, min?: any, max?: any, sum?: number, mean?: number, median?: number}
Overload.descr: Key figures of *field* over *rows* (nil values left out): `count`, `distinct`, `min` and `max` (also for dates and text), and for numbers `sum`, `mean` and `median`. Returns {count: integer, distinct: integer, min?: any, max?: any, sum?: number, mean?: number, median?: number} — The figures.
Make another database the active one, as the toolbar dropdown does. The active filter is cleared.

The tables and views of the active database (or the one named by the `database` option), for use with opensak.sql(). The macro's TEMP tables and views are included. Returns string[] — Table and view names, sorted.
OpenSAK's folder inside the system temp folder (read and write permission by default), without a trailing separator. "/" works as separator on every platform. Returns string — Folder path.
Decode Base64 (GSAK's MimeDecode); white space and line breaks in it are ignored. Invalid Base64 is an error. Returns string — The decoded text.
Base64-encode text (GSAK's MimeEncode). Returns string — The Base64 text.

Split one CSV line into its fields (GSAK's CsvGet): a field in double quotes may contain the separator, and `""` inside quotes is one quote. For a whole file use opensak.read_csv(). Returns string[] — The fields.
Cross sum: the sum of all digits; other characters are ignored. Returns integer — Sum of the digits.

The number behind a geocaching.com code (GSAK's GsCodeToNum): up to GCFFFF the code is hexadecimal, from GCG000 on it is base 31. Works for TB, GL and other two-letter prefixes too; any case. Returns integer? — The number; nil if *code* is not a geocaching.com code.
Decode HTML entities such as `&`, `ä` and `ä` and keep everything else, tags included (GSAK's EntityDecode). opensak.text.html_to_text() also removes the tags. Returns string — The decoded text.

Turn HTML (e.g. a cache description) into plain text: tags removed, entities decoded, block elements and `
` become line breaks. Returns string — The text.
The geocaching.com code for a number (GSAK's NumToGsCode), the reverse of opensak.text.gc_to_id(). Returns string — The code.
Lower case for all letters, not only ASCII (see opensak.text.upper()). Returns string — The text in lower case.

Make a string safe as a database or file name on every platform: characters such as `\ / : * ? " < > |` become `_`, white space is collapsed, leading/trailing dots and spaces are removed and the length is limited to 100. Never empty. Returns string — The safe name.
ROT13 as used for hints. Text in [square brackets] stays unchanged, like on geocaching.com. Returns string — The decoded (or encoded) text.

Like `string.sub`, but counting characters instead of bytes, so it never cuts an ü or é in half (GSAK's Left, Right and SubStr). Positions start at 1; negative ones count from the end; both ends are included. `utf8.len(s)` gives the number of characters. Returns string — The characters from i to j.

Remove white space at the start and end, including line breaks and Unicode spaces such as the no-break space that `%s` in a Lua pattern does not match (GSAK's Alltrim). Returns string — The trimmed text.
Upper case for all letters, not only ASCII: `string.upper` and `s:upper()` leave ä, é, ø … as they are. ß becomes SS. Returns string — The text in upper case.
Decode `%XX` sequences, and `+` as a space as in a query string. Returns string — The decoded text.
Percent-encode text for a URL, e.g. a search term in a link: everything except letters, digits and `-._~` becomes `%XX` of its UTF-8 bytes (GSAK's HttpEncode). Returns string — The encoded text.
Letter value sum (A=1 … Z=26). Accents are dropped (Ä counts as A); other characters are ignored. Returns integer — Sum of the letter values.

The trackables of a cache, each with its `id` for opensak.update_trackable() and the fields listed under Logs, waypoints, attributes and trackables. Missing data is nil. Returns opensak.Trackable[]? — nil if the cache is not in the database.

Run *fn* as one transaction: every change it makes to the active database (opensak.update, insert, delete, sql_write, set_corrected, clear_corrected and the functions for logs, waypoints, ...) is kept when *fn* returns, and all of it is undone if *fn* raises an error, which opensak.transaction() then raises again. Many changes in one transaction are also faster than the same changes committed one by one. Inside *fn*, opensak.cache, caches, sql and the like see the changes already made, except the columns OpenSAK maintains (counts, log dates, distance), which are recalculated once before the commit or when opensak.resync() is called; everything else in OpenSAK, exports included, sees them only afterwards. A transaction inside another one is undone on its own on an error, and kept with the outer one otherwise. opensak.switch_database, move_caches and copy_caches cannot be used inside. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). A macro that ends inside a transaction (e.g. cancelled) keeps none of it. Returns any... — What *fn* returns.

Change fields of a cache in the active database. The keys are cache field names (see Changing caches); only the given fields change. `false` clears a field that is not a boolean. Fields OpenSAK maintains itself, such as `code`, `distance` or `log_count`, cannot be written. Locked caches can be changed too: the lock only protects from imports. Before a macro's first change, OpenSAK asks the user to allow that macro (see Changing caches). Returns boolean — false if the cache is not in the database.

Change fields of a attribute in the active database; only the given fields change, and `false` clears a field that is not required or a boolean. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean — false if there is no attribute with this id.

Change fields of a log in the active database; only the given fields change, and `false` clears a field that is not required or a boolean. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean — false if there is no log with this id.

Change fields of a trackable in the active database; only the given fields change, and `false` clears a field that is not required or a boolean. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean — false if there is no trackable with this id.

Change fields of a waypoint in the active database; only the given fields change, and `false` clears a field that is not required or a boolean. Needs the user's permission like opensak.update(). Returns boolean — false if there is no waypoint with this id.
The OpenSAK version this macro runs in. Returns string — Version, e.g. "1.21.0-beta.3".

The waypoint type for a type name (any case) or a waypoint prefix ("PK", "S1", "F"), with its usual prefix (GSAK's ChildType). Returns string?, string? — The waypoint type and its usual prefix; nil if it is unknown.
The child waypoint types, as in the waypoint dialog, each with its usual prefix — e.g. for opensak.insert_waypoint(). Returns {name: string, prefix: string}[] — One table per waypoint type.

The waypoints of a cache, each with its `id` for opensak.update_waypoint() and the fields listed under Logs, waypoints, attributes and trackables. Missing data is nil. Returns opensak.Waypoint[]? — nil if the cache is not in the database.

Write *text* to a file as UTF-8 and return the file written. A relative path is resolved against the macro file's folder. The folder needs write permission (the OpenSAK temp folder, opensak.temp_dir(), has it by default); for an unapproved one the user is asked first. Only these file types can be written: .txt .csv .tsv .html .htm .svg .md .json. An existing file is replaced, or extended with `append = true`. At most 20 MB. Returns string — The file written (full path).
CPU time used by OpenSAK, in seconds. Returns number — Seconds.

Seconds since the epoch, now or for a table {year, month, day, hour, min, sec}. Returns integer — Seconds since the epoch.
